unit.title: Swift bootcamp: values, contracts and retrieval
unit.summary: Build value and object types. Learn construction, errors, closures, and protocols, then combine them in a tested core.

lessons.title: Edit structs and make shared state visible
lessons.summary: Build value models, mark changes with mutating and inout, and spot when a copied value still reaches a shared object.
objectives: Create a struct and predict its member access and assigned copies.
Explain mutating on a method and inout with & at a call.
Recognize overlapping storage access and shared class references inside a value.

sections.title: Make a draft an independent value
sections.html:
A struct defines a value type: a kind of value with stored properties and methods. A property is data belonging to an instance, one constructed value of that type. An initializer creates the instance with starting state. Dot syntax reads a member, such as draft.name. Assigning a struct gives value semantics, so editing one copy does not change another’s value fields. This resembles making a Kotlin data-class draft, but Swift needs no generated copy call. A type declaration describes how to make values; it is not one shared global object.

Kotlin data class generates conveniences such as copy and equality for specified primary-constructor properties. Swift struct is not exactly that bundle: assignment provides value semantics, a simple memberwise initializer can be synthesized, and equality/hash support requires appropriate protocol conformance. You do not call an automatically generated copy method just because Kotlin taught that pattern. Let/var still matters: a let-bound struct cannot change a stored part of its value, even if that property was declared var. A var-bound struct can mutate properties that permit it. Thread safety, validation and deep cloning remain separate design decisions.

sections.title: Mark the method that changes the value
sections.html:
A mutating method can change the struct value it is called on. Here name and count are stored var properties. The memberwise initializer is a compiler-provided constructor taking those properties by name. AddOne changes count, so it needs mutating. Caption only reads state, so it does not. Original is fixed with let; edited is a writable var copied from it. Changing edited.name and adding one leave original alone. The output is Ada: 1 and Rae: 2. The method’s mutation permission does not override the caller’s let binding.

struct Draft {
    var name: String
    var count: Int

    mutating func addOne() {
        count += 1
    }

    func caption() -> String {
        return "\(name): \(count)"
    }
}
let original = Draft(name: "Ada", count: 1)
var edited = original
edited.name = "Rae"
edited.addOne()
print(original.caption())
print(edited.caption())

Lowercase self names the current instance. It can distinguish a stored property from a parameter with the same name. Uppercase Self names a type relationship, explained in lesson 069. Mutating methods may also replace self with another value of the same type; that is still caller-visible value mutation. A method without mutating cannot directly assign stored properties of a struct. A class method has reference semantics and different mutation rules, introduced below and in lesson 066. Attempting original.addOne is rejected at compile time, because modifying a let-bound struct conflicts with the binding contract. Calling its read-only caption is fine. An initializer supplies state; it is not an arbitrary method named after the type.

sections.title: Show caller-visible edits at both ends
sections.html:
An inout parameter gives a function temporary mutable access to a caller’s writable storage. It is written in the declaration and marked with & at the call. Count starts at two and becomes five after add receives three. A literal or let-bound value cannot supply that writable access. A normal Int parameter is an immutable local input and cannot replace the caller’s integer. This block uses Draft from above for renamed, though the add/count part runs independently. Renamed shows another design: edit a local value and return it for the caller to store.

func add(_ amount: Int, to value: inout Int) {
    value += amount
}
var count = 2
add(3, to: &count)
print(count)

func renamed(_ draft: Draft, to name: String) -> Draft {
    var result = draft
    result.name = name
    return result
}

Renamed takes a regular Draft input, makes a local var copy, edits it, and returns the result. The caller chooses whether to keep it. Inout instead behaves semantically like reading the input and writing the final value back, even when the compiler optimizes storage access. It is not a general C pointer or an ordinary Kotlin object reference. Its access must end with the call; an escaping closure, one that can outlive the call, cannot keep the parameter for later mutation. Use inout for a clear synchronous edit. Return a new value when that makes ownership and composition easier to follow.

sections.title: Allow one incompatible access at a time
sections.html:
Exclusivity means a modifying access cannot overlap another incompatible access to the same storage. Inout holds that access for the call. A mutating method needs it for its receiver, the value on which the method runs. Passing one variable to two inout parameters requests two overlapping modifications. Swift rejects that even if this particular algorithm seems harmless. Some conflicts are detected before execution; others are checked at runtime. The rule describes storage access during the call. It does not create a lock or make shared state safe across threads.

Suppose balance(_ left: inout Int, _ right: inout Int) adjusts two balances. Calling balance(&count, &count) is invalid. Repair the intended algorithm: if two independent values are needed, make independent variables and write back deliberately. If swapping positions of one array is the goal, use swapAt instead of taking two overlapping subscripts as inout through the same container. Disjoint stored properties of some locally provable value storage can be permitted, but do not depend on that optimization without understanding the access rule. Exclusivity is about overlapping access, not a mutex or actor. Safe synchronous mutation does not automatically establish race-free use across threads.

sections.title: Check what a copied value contains
sections.html:
A class is a reference type: values of that type refer to an object with identity. Packet is still a struct, but its note stores a reference to one Note object. Copying Packet gives independent title fields while both packets refer to that same note. Changing second.title affects only second. Changing second.note.text affects the shared Note, so first sees Shared too. === asks whether the references identify the same object and returns true. The outputs are One, Shared, and true. Final prevents subclasses of Note; it does not freeze its text.

final class Note {
    var text = "Initial"
}
struct Packet {
    var title: String
    let note: Note
}
let first = Packet(title: "One", note: Note())
var second = first
second.title = "Two"
second.note.text = "Shared"
print(first.title)
print(first.note.text)
print(first.note === second.note)

Let fixes Packet’s stored value, including its note reference. It does not freeze the reached Note object, so that object’s var text can change. Replacing a Packet field would be a different edit. Kotlin data-class copy also retains nested object references, but Swift’s outer value assignment needs no copy method. If drafts need independent nested state, use nested value types or an explicit policy for constructing independent objects. Copy-on-write arrays containing class references still copy those references as references. A struct wrapper does not make all reachable state immutable, safe to transfer across concurrency boundaries, or safe for simultaneous access.

sections.title: Find the value edit boundary in real code
sections.html:
A mutation boundary is the place where an operation is allowed to change a value. The question model is a struct with let fields, so callers cannot directly change those stored fields. Hashable gives equality and hashing for lookup; it does not promise a deep copy. BeforeAfter marks its update methods mutating. The ReportAnIssue helper takes inout BeforeAfter, making the caller-visible edit explicit. Its key paths name properties and need separate study. You can already recognize the edit permission without claiming to understand or have tested every part of the utility.

Misconceptions include assuming every var property can be changed through a let struct, assuming an ampersand is a reusable pointer, diagnosing an exclusivity error as a threading bug, and assuming a nested class was cloned. Classify the corresponding evidence: compiler rejection, temporary-access lifetime, overlapping synchronous storage access, and shared identity. Inout and mutating are related but not interchangeable spellings: one describes a parameter contract, the other a value method’s receiver mutation. We verified these anchors and target globs, not the entire utility implementation or company app. The exercise checks small deterministic edit boundaries with no unsafe overlap execution.

quiz.explanation: inout and ampersand describe caller-visible temporary access. They provide no retained pointer or scheduling contract.

quiz.explanation: Outer value fields remain independent, but a stored class reference continues to identify its shared object.

exercise.brief: Write a value counter with a mutating method and an inout edit. Explain the separate shared-object case.
steps: Declare Counter with a writable value and mutating increment().
Copy a let original into var edited. Increment only edited.
Write add(_ amount: Int, to value: inout Int). Call it with &edited.value.
Explain on paper why one variable cannot supply two overlapping inout arguments.
Run the Note/Packet example separately. Identify independent fields and the shared Note identity.
acceptance: Original remains two while edited becomes six after increment and adding three.
Mutation is explicit at the method and inout call sites.
No overlapping inout operation or unsafe pointer is executed.
The explanation labels value fields and reference identity separately.
exercise.solution:
This counter answer runs by itself. It needs no declaration from the earlier sections. Original starts at two and stays fixed; edited permits changes. Predict the result after one increment and an inout addition of three. The final array edit uses one swapAt operation instead of overlapping inout accesses.

struct Counter {
    var value: Int
    mutating func increment() { value += 1 }
}
func add(_ amount: Int, to value: inout Int) {
    value += amount
}
let original = Counter(value: 2)
var edited = original
edited.increment()
add(3, to: &edited.value)
print(original.value)
print(edited.value)
var positions = [1, 2]
positions.swapAt(0, 1)
print(positions)

Output is two, six and [2, 1]. The method modifies only edited. The inout call temporarily mutates its writable property and ends before the subsequent print. SwapAt expresses one container operation without two overlapping inout subscript accesses. Explain the invalid same-variable call in notes rather than inserting it into the working program.

For changed-input retrieval, start at four, increment twice and add one. Predict the original and edited values before running. Then contrast this counter with Packet containing Note: the shared class state requires a separate policy even though the wrapper is a value. The result is evidence of small language behavior, not a completed client mutation, concurrency proof, or automatic mastery of value ownership.

lessons.title: Create valid values and choose how properties behave
lessons.summary: Set valid starting state, compare stored and calculated properties, and control who can read or change them.
objectives: Explain properties that store, compute, observe, or delay a value.
Write initializers that can fail and know when Swift supplies one.
Separate access permission, setter permission, mutation, and thread safety.

sections.title: Set the rules when a value is created
sections.html:
A stored property holds data in an instance. An initializer, written init, sets the starting state so every required property has a value before the instance can be used. A default in the property declaration can do some of that work. This plays a role like an Android constructor, but follows Swift’s own rules. Successful construction produces an instance when you call the type. The initializer does not use an ordinary return expression to produce that instance. A validation rule should be clear at the creation boundary.

Swift can synthesize a memberwise initializer, meaning it generates a constructor from the stored fields. A custom initializer in a struct’s primary declaration removes that automatic memberwise initializer. Defining one in an extension can preserve synthesis where the other rules allow it. Do not assume the Kotlin primary-constructor and copy pattern applies. An invariant is a rule that must stay true, such as a label being nonempty. Enforce it at construction, then restrict later setters or expose checked edit methods if mutation could break it. A valid starting value and a value that stays valid throughout its lifetime are separate requirements.

sections.title: Reject an invalid starting value safely
sections.html:
A failable initializer can return nil when it cannot create a valid instance. The question mark in init? marks this permission. Guard rejects a candidate that is zero or negative before storing anything as a valid PositiveQuantity. self.value names the instance property; candidate names the input. The underscore removes the call-site argument label. Doubled is a computed property: reading it runs a getter, code that calculates an answer. It stores no separate doubled number. The valid input three prints three and six; rejected zero gives nil.

struct PositiveQuantity {
    let value: Int

    init?(_ candidate: Int) {
        guard candidate > 0 else { return nil }
        self.value = candidate
    }

    var doubled: Int {
        return value * 2
    }
}
if let quantity = PositiveQuantity(3) {
    print(quantity.value)
    print(quantity.doubled)
}
print(PositiveQuantity(0) == nil)

The optional binding applies to the constructed value, just as it did to String? and dictionary lookup. A failable initializer can only convey failure as absence; a throwing initializer in lesson 067 can preserve an error reason. The name PositiveQuantity does not by itself guarantee doubling every possible positive Int avoids overflow. Domain bounds for arithmetic need their own policy; our small test input stays within them. A custom primary initializer means callers cannot assume a synthesized PositiveQuantity(value:) call exists. Calling the declared API is part of maintaining the invariant, not an incidental syntax preference.

sections.title: Tell calculation from assignment observation
sections.html:
A getter calculates what a property returns; a setter handles a proposed new value. An observer runs around assignment to a property. Meter.value stores an integer. willSet sees the proposed value as newValue before assignment, and didSet sees the previous value as oldValue afterward. Even assigning the same value can trigger them. Ordinary direct assignments that first initialize this type’s own stored properties do not run these observers; inherited or delegated setter paths need separate care. Meter() starts with zero. The later assignment of three runs the observers.

struct Meter {
    var value = 0 {
        willSet { print("Next \(newValue)") }
        didSet { print("Previous \(oldValue)") }
    }

    var doubled: Int {
        get { value * 2 }
        set { value = newValue / 2 }
    }
}
var meter = Meter()
meter.value = 3
print(meter.doubled)
meter.doubled = 10
print(meter.value)

Doubled declares get and set, so it stores no independent integer. The getter returns twice value. The setter receives a proposed doubled value as newValue and assigns half to value, triggering the stored property’s observers. The printed computed value is six, then the final stored value is five. Integer truncation means setting an odd doubled amount would not round-trip exactly; specify the desired contract rather than assuming property syntax guarantees inverse operations. Kotlin custom accessors are a useful analogy, but Swift newValue/oldValue and initialization rules must be read directly. Observers are not locks, transactions, or a general validation rollback mechanism.

sections.title: Choose current text or a saved first-read value
sections.html:
A lazy stored property waits until its first read to initialize its value. FirstCaption therefore uses count two when first accessed, then keeps that String. Updating count to four does not rebuild it. LiveCaption is computed, so its getter reads count on each access and returns Count 4 at the end. The lazy value prints First 2 twice. Lazy needs var because its stored state is established later. On a struct, that first read can mutate storage, so the draft binding must also permit mutation. A let draft cannot authorize that access.

struct CaptionDraft {
    var count = 1
    var liveCaption: String { "Count \(count)" }
    lazy var firstCaption: String = "First \(count)"
}
var draft = CaptionDraft()
draft.count = 2
print(draft.firstCaption)
draft.count = 4
print(draft.firstCaption)
print(draft.liveCaption)

Kotlin lazy helps explain waiting for the first read, but Swift lazy has no equivalent built-in synchronization promise. Concurrent first reads are not guaranteed to initialize exactly once safely. Choose isolation or another synchronization mechanism when access can overlap. A closure used during lazy initialization can also retain an owner; laziness does not make captures weak. State which freshness rule you need: first-read storage, calculation on every read, or a cache with explicit invalidation. They are different designs. This small run checks first-read behavior; it does not benchmark work or test races.

sections.title: Say who may read, construct, and write
sections.html:
An access level controls where a declaration can be used. A module is a separately built unit of code. Internal, Swift’s default, allows use inside that module. Public allows importing modules to use an API, the declarations offered to callers. Private limits access to the enclosing declaration and eligible same-file extensions; fileprivate gives file scope. Package access allows use across modules in the same package. These boundaries differ from Kotlin internal and Java package access. Check the actual module before translating the words. Access permission does not create synchronization or thread safety.

A public struct does not automatically get a public memberwise initializer, even if its stored properties are public. Write an explicit public init when an importing module must construct it. public private(set) var count permits public reads while limiting setter access. Let disallows reassignment of storage or a binding; private(set) limits who may write a var. They are different rules. Open adds permission for external subclassing or overriding in class APIs; lesson 066 covers that. None adds actors or locks. A testing-enabled @testable import permits internal access, not arbitrary private access. Check construction and mutation separately.

sections.title: Inspect the actual creation API
sections.html:
A public type is visible outside its module, but that does not make all its members public. The linked question model is public while its stored fields and navigation property use internal visibility. Its memberwise initializer, the constructor Swift derives from fields, is not automatically public either. The linked BeforeAfter type instead declares public initializers and keeps implementation storage private. Its before and after properties are computed views of that storage. Those declarations show intended caller access. They do not by themselves tell you the runtime cost of each read.

Misconceptions include treating a computed property as cached, expecting a lazy caption to stay current, assuming observers validate construction, and assuming public on a type exports all synthesis. A compiler diagnostic for accessing a lazy struct property through let needs a mutation explanation, not a blanket var conversion across the app. A stale lazy display needs a freshness policy, not repeated initializer calls. The optional initialization-access supplement covers class delegation, wider access and additional property cases after this core lesson. It is matching further detail; the standalone examples here contain the prerequisites needed for today’s exercise without requiring the old advanced core.

options: No, its getter runs on access
quiz.explanation: Property syntax alone does not provide a cache. Separate stored/lazy/cache contracts must establish retained results.

quiz.question: Why must a lazy property be var?
options: Its stored value is established on first access after initialization
Because it always changes on each read
quiz.explanation: Deferred first initialization modifies storage. It does not imply repeated recalculation or synchronization.

quiz.question: Does public struct synthesize a public memberwise initializer?
options: Only if all fields are public
No, an explicit exported construction API is needed
quiz.explanation: The synthesized memberwise initializer is not automatically public. Defining a deliberate public init exposes the intended boundary.

exercise.brief: Create a label only when its text is nonempty. Compare a current caption with a saved first-read caption.
steps: Declare Label with let text and init? that rejects the empty String.
Handle both valid and invalid construction without force unwrapping.
Make a mutable draft with a count, a computed current caption, and a lazy first caption.
Read first at count two. Change count to four and read both captions.
Explain which declarations and explicit initializer another module would need if Label became public.
acceptance: Empty construction yields nil and valid construction preserves the text.
The first-read caption remains based on count two.
The computed caption reflects count four.
The access explanation includes an explicit public initializer rather than inferred synthesis.
exercise.solution:
This standalone answer separates two rules: whether a Label can be created and whether a caption stays current. The types need no UI framework. Predict what happens to an empty label, and which text reflects count four after first has already been read.

struct Label {
    let text: String
    init?(_ text: String) {
        guard !text.isEmpty else { return nil }
        self.text = text
    }
}
struct Draft {
    var count = 0
    var current: String { "Now \(count)" }
    lazy var first: String = "First \(count)"
}
print(Label("") == nil)
if let label = Label("Ada") { print(label.text) }
var draft = Draft()
draft.count = 2
print(draft.first)
draft.count = 4
print(draft.first)
print(draft.current)

Expected output is true, Ada, First 2, First 2 and Now 4. The local parameter text shadows the stored property name, so self.text identifies the destination. The validation rejects exactly empty input, not whitespace; add a separately stated policy if the product needs trimming. A lazy value is not invalidated by changing count.

For an exported version, choose public on the type and intended readable member, then explicitly mark the initializer public. That is a language-contract explanation here, not a claim that a two-module build ran. Try a changed test input and note which properties recompute versus retain state. The optional supplement broadens the topic, while independent practice and observed output remain the evidence of learning.

lessons.title: Share class objects and use subclass behavior safely
lessons.summary: Follow class identity, subclass initialization, method overrides, and safe checks of an object’s actual type.
objectives: Predict when two class bindings refer to the same object.
Build a subclass and explain its initializer paths and override.
Use is and as? without confusing an object’s identity with its declared type.

sections.title: Choose shared identity when you need it
sections.html:
A class is a reference type. Its bindings refer to objects with identity, so two bindings can reach the same object. Assignment copies that reference rather than making an independent object. This fits an Android controller or service with a shared lifetime. Let fixes which object a binding refers to, but the object’s var properties can still change. That differs from directly editing a let-bound struct. Choose class or struct from the desired behavior: do callers need one shared object, or independently editable values? Familiar syntax alone is a weak reason.

Classes can inherit from one superclass and can conform to multiple protocols. Structs and enums do not inherit from classes. Inheritance lets a specialized instance reuse and override a superclass contract; it also creates construction and access obligations. Kotlin classes are final by default, whereas a Swift class can be subclassed within its permitted access boundary unless declared final. Swift public allows external use, while open grants relevant external subclassing/overriding permission. Do not introduce inheritance merely to reuse a formatter; composition or a protocol may express a capability more directly. Today’s hierarchy is a small learning test input, not a recommendation for every domain model.

sections.title: Compare objects by identity
sections.html:
Identity asks whether two references reach the very same object. Swift writes that check as ===. Counter has a default stored value, so Counter() can initialize it. Final means the class cannot have subclasses. First and second are let bindings referring to one Counter; second.value can become three without changing either reference. First therefore sees three too. Third is a newly constructed Counter whose value also becomes three. Its matching value does not give it matching identity: the two identity checks print true, then false.

final class Counter {
    var value = 0
}
let first = Counter()
let second = first
second.value = 3
print(first.value)
print(first === second)
let third = Counter()
third.value = 3
print(first === third)

Kotlin/Java object references provide a close assignment analogy, but equality spellings differ: Kotlin referential equality uses three equals, Java double equals checks reference identity, and Swift uses three equals for class identity. Do not mechanically port the same punctuation between languages. Reference semantics do not provide a lock or guarantee immutable service state. Two aliases can mutate one object, so later concurrency lessons must establish an owner/isolation contract. If independent edit state is the requirement, a value model may be simpler. If shared identity and lifetime are intentional, explicitly name who owns that object and who merely observes it.

sections.title: Initialize a subclass and override a method
sections.html:
A superclass is a base class; a subclass extends it. An override supplies specialized behavior for an inherited method. Record stores name and marks its name initializer required, so subclasses must support that construction shape through allowed inheritance or implementation. TaggedRecord adds tag. Its full initializer sets tag before calling the superclass initializer. Its convenience initializer supplies zero and delegates to another initializer on the same class. Override marks caption as specialized behavior. super.caption() still calls the base implementation when assembling the tagged text.

class Record {
    let name: String

    required init(name: String) {
        self.name = name
    }

    func caption() -> String {
        return name
    }
}
final class TaggedRecord: Record {
    let tag: Int

    init(name: String, tag: Int) {
        self.tag = tag
        super.init(name: name)
    }

    required convenience init(name: String) {
        self.init(name: name, tag: 0)
    }

    override func caption() -> String {
        return "\(super.caption()) [\(tag)]"
    }
}
let record: Record = TaggedRecord(name: "Ada", tag: 7)
print(record.caption())

Static type is the type declared for a binding; dynamic type is the object’s actual runtime type. Here record is declared Record but holds a TaggedRecord. Dynamic dispatch chooses the override and prints Ada [7]. This is an inherited-method call, not a cast or enum switch. Final prevents more subclasses of TaggedRecord. The designated initializer sets tag before super.init because its introduced stored state must be established first. This standalone hierarchy needs no NSObject or UI framework. Referring to the object through Record does not make a new base object or discard its tag. The underlying instance remains the same.

sections.title: Follow the initializer’s delegation path
sections.html:
A designated initializer is a main construction path for a class. It initializes introduced stored properties and calls a designated initializer of the immediate superclass when one exists. A convenience initializer delegates to another initializer on the same class, eventually reaching a designated path. Delegation means asking that other initializer to complete its part. Two-phase initialization first establishes the stored state across the hierarchy, then allows full instance use and customization. Do not read unfinished self or let it escape early. Kotlin constructors offer useful orientation, but Swift checks its own initialization order.

Class initializer inheritance is conditional, unlike simply inheriting every ordinary method. Inspect the full initializer set before assuming a convenience overload is available on a subclass. Overriding a nonrequired superclass designated initializer uses override; implementing a required shape uses required. Failable init? can represent ordinary construction failure, while a deliberate fatalError in an unsupported coder initializer represents a programmer restriction and traps. It is not equivalent to validating user input and returning nil. The initialization-access supplement expands these contracts, but the complete hierarchy above supplies today’s needed construction rules. For a value type there is no superclass and no class convenience/designated hierarchy.

sections.title: Ask for a narrower view without making a new object
sections.html:
A conditional downcast asks whether an existing object can be viewed as a more specific type. as? returns an optional answer. This example uses Record and TaggedRecord from above. The first array entry is only a Record, so the cast returns nil and prints Base only. The second is a TaggedRecord, so the bound tagged view reads tag nine. It is the same object, not a clone. is asks the type question as Bool and prints false, then true. A compatible view as the superclass needs no conditional test.

let records: [Record] = [
    Record(name: "Base"),
    TaggedRecord(name: "Special", tag: 9)
]
for record in records {
    if let tagged = record as? TaggedRecord {
        print("Tag \(tagged.tag)")
    } else {
        print("Base only")
    }
}
print(records[0] is TaggedRecord)
print(records[1] is TaggedRecord)

A forced as! downcast traps when the actual type does not fit. Use as? for an ordinary subtype question in a mixed list. Plain as supports compatible views such as upcasts and some bridges; it is not a universal number-conversion operation. If the consumer only needs behavior, prefer a promised method over repeated subtype tests. Frequent casts may show that the abstraction is missing a capability. Kotlin is and as? offer similar intent, but Swift class, protocol, and bridging rules remain separate. Uppercase Any can hold unrelated values; lesson 069 distinguishes that from protocol-bound any.

sections.title: Separate language rules from UI behavior
sections.html:
An inherited method belongs to a superclass and may be overridden by a subclass. The cancellation controller overrides viewDidLoad and calls super before installing callbacks. Its state initializer delegates to super. The required coder initializer deliberately traps because that construction path is unsupported. These are real language patterns inside UIKit, Apple’s iOS UI framework; running the controller needs an iOS target and its dependencies. The helper uses as? before a modal-specific hide call. That cast narrows the existing controller reference. It does not construct a different screen.

Misconceptions include expecting let to freeze a class, assuming upcasting slices off subclass state, using as! as input validation, and presuming all superclass initializers are inherited. The correct next check depends on the symptom: identify aliases for surprising mutation, dynamic method behavior for superclass access, optional downcast failure for an unexpected subtype, and declared initializer paths for unavailable calls. We verified source membership via the active cancellation target glob. We did not build UIKit code, verify controller lifecycle timing, or migrate the hierarchy. Choose composition or protocols when capabilities, rather than inherited identity, are the real requirement.

exercise.brief: Build a caption base class and a tagged subclass. Check method behavior and downcasts through base references.
steps: Create Record with required init(name:) and caption().
Create TaggedRecord with tag, a full designated initializer, and a required convenience initializer taking only name.
Override caption and use super.caption() when making its result.
Put a base object and a tagged object in [Record]. Print captions and read tags only after a successful conditional cast.
Explain identity and initialization order. Use no forced casts.
acceptance: Base caption is Base and tagged caption is Ada [7].
The required convenience path creates tag zero.
Conditional casting fails safely for the base and succeeds for the subclass.
No UIKit imports, forced casts or partially initialized self escape are required.
exercise.solution:
This complete answer repeats the declarations so you can run it separately. It tests both construction paths and calls through the base type, rather than checking only the concrete subclass. Predict which iteration prints a tag and whether a successful cast keeps the original identity.

class Record {
    let name: String
    required init(name: String) { self.name = name }
    func caption() -> String { name }
}
final class TaggedRecord: Record {
    let tag: Int
    init(name: String, tag: Int) {
        self.tag = tag
        super.init(name: name)
    }
    required convenience init(name: String) {
        self.init(name: name, tag: 0)
    }
    override func caption() -> String { "\(super.caption()) [\(tag)]" }
}
let base = Record(name: "Base")
let tagged = TaggedRecord(name: "Ada", tag: 7)
let records: [Record] = [base, tagged]
for record in records {
    print(record.caption())
    if let special = record as? TaggedRecord { print(special.tag) }
}
print(TaggedRecord(name: "Default").tag)
print((records[1] as? TaggedRecord) === tagged)

Output is Base, Ada [7], seven, zero and true. The first iteration has no tag line, because the cast returns nil. The last check confirms that the successful cast still refers to tagged’s original instance. The base-typed call uses the override, proving that changing the static view did not change the dynamic object.

lessons.title: Name outcomes, keep error reasons, and clean up on exit
lessons.summary: Use enums for distinct states, throw errors with useful reasons, and understand when defer runs cleanup.
objectives: Create and match enum cases with data, and compare them with fixed raw values.
Read throws, try, do, and catch, and explain what try? loses.
Predict which defer blocks are registered and the order in which they run.

sections.title: Use one named state at a time
sections.html:
An enum defines a type with a fixed set of named cases. An associated value is data carried by a particular case, such as loaded names or a failure message. One enum value holds one case at a time. This avoids contradictory loading and error flags, much like a Kotlin sealed state. The type controls which state shapes can exist; it does not decide which transitions are legal. Swift cases are variants of a value type, not sealed subclass instances. Data inside a case can still include shared class references.

Kotlin sealed subclasses are a helpful modeling analogy, but Swift enum cases are variants of one value type rather than subclass instances. Associated payloads can themselves contain class references, so outer value semantics still do not imply deep cloning. Begin with made-up idle, loaded names and failed reason. Successful empty names remain loaded with an empty array, not failed and not idle. Distinguishing these outcomes preserves the user’s next action. The standard Error protocol identifies values usable as thrown errors; an enum can conform to it while carrying precise failure data. No networking framework or old course prerequisite is necessary.

sections.title: Match every state and read its data
sections.html:
Pattern matching asks which enum case is present and extracts its data. Outcome declares idle, loaded with names, and failed with a message. Equatable requests value comparison; Swift can generate it here because all case data supports equality. The switch handles all three cases and needs no default. case let .loaded(names) creates a local immutable binding for the payload; it does not cast to a subclass. A leading dot during construction works because the function parameter supplies the expected Outcome type. Empty loaded names print No matches; failure prints Retry: offline.

enum Outcome: Equatable {
    case idle
    case loaded(names: [String])
    case failed(message: String)
}
func caption(for outcome: Outcome) -> String {
    switch outcome {
    case .idle:
        return "Start"
    case let .loaded(names):
        return names.isEmpty ? "No matches" : names.joined(separator: ", ")
    case let .failed(message):
        return "Retry: \(message)"
    }
}
print(caption(for: .loaded(names: [])))
print(caption(for: .failed(message: "offline")))

The output is No matches then Retry: offline. Adding a local offline case requires this exhaustive switch to account for it. Default can hide that new decision, so use it only for an intentional catch-all policy. if case let can extract one variant when ignoring the others is appropriate; rendering every state usually deserves a full switch. Equatable does not validate message content, enforce legal transitions, perform analytics or cancel requests. Updating an enum’s state means assigning a new case value; a failed payload is not a mutable property shared by every possible case.

sections.title: Keep fixed codes separate from changing payloads
sections.html:
A raw value is one fixed value assigned to each enum case. ReasonCode uses String raw values, so every offline case has the same code offline. rawValue reads that code. The initializer ReasonCode(rawValue:) can fail because external text may name no declared case. new_code therefore returns nil. It does not invent a new case. Decide whether to reject unknown text, preserve it separately, or use an explicit fallback. A forced unwrap would turn this normal compatibility question into a trap.

enum ReasonCode: String {
    case offline = "offline"
    case invalid = "invalid"
}
print(ReasonCode.offline.rawValue)
print(ReasonCode(rawValue: "new_code") == nil)

Associated data instead varies per constructed instance, such as a failure’s original invalid input. A raw-value enum cannot simultaneously declare arbitrary associated payloads. Combine a fixed code with other fields in a struct, or use an associated-value enum with a computed code if the domain requires both. Codable or CaseIterable are separate capabilities and should not be inferred from enum alone. Kotlin enums with constructor fields may look similar to raw codes, but Swift’s raw conversion contract and payload restrictions must be read directly. The exercise uses no real wire response; it demonstrates boundary policy using made-up strings.

sections.title: Mark failure and handle its reason
sections.html:
An error is a value explaining failure. The Error protocol is the language contract for values that can be thrown. Throws lets the function either return normally or throw. Try marks a throwing call but does not catch it. Do encloses code whose thrown errors the following catch clauses handle. This parser first checks whether text becomes an integer, then whether that integer is positive. Its first catch binds the original text for a notInteger failure. The last catch handles other errors. The bad test input prints Invalid integer: bad.

enum QuantityError: Error {
    case notInteger(String)
    case nonpositive(Int)
}
func quantity(from text: String) throws -> Int {
    guard let value = Int(text) else {
        throw QuantityError.notInteger(text)
    }
    guard value > 0 else {
        throw QuantityError.nonpositive(value)
    }
    return value
}
do {
    print(try quantity(from: "bad"))
} catch let QuantityError.notInteger(text) {
    print("Invalid integer: \(text)")
} catch {
    print("Other error: \(error)")
}

Ordinary untyped throws permits failure without listing Java-style checked exception classes. Modern Swift also supports typed throws, but this beginner example does not need it. try? changes a thrown failure into nil, losing its reason. try! traps if an error is thrown. Force unwrapping and failed preconditions can also trap; do/catch does not recover those traps. When a caller must explain invalid input, handle the error explicitly or pass it onward. Do not turn try? into invented success with a fallback. Result is a standard enum storing success or failure as a value; it is a choice, not a requirement for every throwing function.

sections.title: Register cleanup before an exit can happen
sections.html:
Defer registers code to run when its containing scope exits normally, by return, or by throw. Registration happens only if execution reaches the defer statement. This block uses QuantityError from above. Inspect prints Enter, registers outer cleanup, then registers inner cleanup in the do scope. With false, the guard throws: Inner cleanup runs, then Outer cleanup, then the caller prints Handled. Work and After inner scope are skipped. Several defers in the same scope run in reverse registration order. Cleanup follows scope, not only the successful path.

func inspect(_ valid: Bool) throws {
    print("Enter")
    defer { print("Outer cleanup") }
    do {
        defer { print("Inner cleanup") }
        guard valid else { throw QuantityError.nonpositive(0) }
        print("Work")
    }
    print("After inner scope")
}
do {
    try inspect(false)
} catch {
    print("Handled")
}

Kotlin try/finally offers similar cleanup intent, but Swift’s registration point and containing scope matter. Defer does not catch errors, resume tasks, or undo arbitrary mutation. It does not guarantee recovery from process termination. Tie it to one synchronous responsibility, such as releasing a resource that was acquired successfully. Put registration before any later early exit that must release it. Asynchronous resources and task cancellation need separate lifetime rules in later lessons. This print trace checks scope-exit order. It does not show a real file was closed, a production callback was removed, or a canceled operation stopped.

sections.title: Separate error handling, state change, and cleanup
sections.html:
Error handling decides what to do with a thrown failure. It does not undo earlier changes automatically. The linked coordinator’s NavigationState carries question data in one case and no payload in bookingPrompt. CancellationReason instead uses fixed String codes. The response array is explicitly edited on an error path; throwing alone did not roll back an append. The helper registers modal cleanup with defer inside its callback. These anchors show distinct responsibilities: state shape, failure handling, and cleanup. The surrounding async and UIKit machinery needs later study.

Misconceptions include collapsing failed retrieval to loaded([]), confusing a raw code with arbitrary payload, believing try catches, and expecting defer to run only on success. Define expected observations for valid, invalid, empty and unknown-code test inputs. A default catch that prints one message may be an intentional simplification but loses classification unless a separate boundary preserves it. The question is what the caller needs to decide, not which punctuation produces fewer lines. We verified actual source locations and target inclusion without running these company flows. The exercise keeps invalid-input identity visible and checks cleanup on both normal and thrown exits.

exercise.solution:
This standalone answer makes each failure reason visible at the caller. Its cleanup is a printed trace, not proof that a real resource was released. Predict the order for each test input: cleanup runs as parse leaves, before the caller prints acceptance or the matching error message.

enum ParseFailure: Error {
    case invalid(String)
    case nonpositive(Int)
}
func parse(_ text: String) throws -> Int {
    defer { print("Cleanup \(text)") }
    guard let value = Int(text) else { throw ParseFailure.invalid(text) }
    guard value > 0 else { throw ParseFailure.nonpositive(value) }
    return value
}
for text in ["3", "bad", "0"] {
    do {
        let value = try parse(text)
        print("Accepted \(value)")
    } catch let ParseFailure.invalid(original) {
        print("Invalid \(original)")
    } catch let ParseFailure.nonpositive(value) {
        print("Nonpositive \(value)")
    } catch {
        print("Unexpected")
    }
}

Each cleanup line appears before its caller’s Accepted, Invalid or Nonpositive line because parse exits before the caller resumes that path. The reason remains available to the matching catch. An optional fallback to zero would treat as the same parse failure, nonpositive rejection and an invented success sentinel, violating the contract.

For retrieval, add a negative test input and predict the nonpositive payload. Then add a locally declared enum variant and identify which switches or catch classifications need an intentional decision. Exhaustiveness and error effects constrain structure, while business transitions and recovery policy remain your responsibility. Your independent parser and trace provide learning evidence; this worked code does not complete practice or establish app error reporting.

lessons.title: Read closures and follow who keeps an owner alive
lessons.summary: Store function values, compare live and snapshot captures, and test a callback before and after its owner is released.
objectives: Read a closure’s inputs, result, and call syntax.
Explain escaping as a lifetime permission, separate from scheduling.
Draw strong and weak ownership and check a saved callback with a missing owner.

sections.title: Ask what a stored callback keeps alive
sections.html:
A callback is a function value another object can call later. A closure can capture, or use, names from its surrounding scope. Its type describes inputs and result; its captures affect what it keeps alive. This is familiar from an Android listener, where you ask who stores it and who removes it. In Swift, also ask what the stored closure owns. These facts do not tell you its thread, actor, call count, or cancellation policy. The examples run synchronously so ownership can be studied without uncertain event timing.

Automatic Reference Counting, or ARC, keeps a class object alive while strong references own it. An unreachable circle of strong references can therefore survive after external owners disappear. A tracing garbage collector, such as on the JVM, can collect a circle unreachable from its roots. A listener still reachable from a singleton can leak under either system. The difference matters when an owner stores a closure that strongly captures that owner. Draw the owning edges from owner to stored closure and back to owner. Then decide whether one edge should be released or made weak, based on the required lifetime.

sections.title: Read the full function type first
sections.html:
A function type describes inputs and output. (Int) -> String accepts an integer and returns text. Inspect receives that operation, calls it during its own execution, and prints the result. Caption stores a closure of that type. Its braces hold the body, value names its input, in starts the body, and return sends back text. The first call passes the stored function. The second supplies a trailing closure after the call; one expression needs no explicit return. The outputs are Count 3 and Next 4.

func inspect(_ value: Int, using operation: (Int) -> String) {
    print(operation(value))
}
let caption: (Int) -> String = { value in
    return "Count \(value)"
}
inspect(3, using: caption)
inspect(4) { value in
    "Next \(value)"
}

There is no asynchronous scheduling here. Void would describe no useful result, for example () -> Void for a zero-argument action. A property (() -> Void)? is an optional function value; action?() invokes it only if present. That optional check says nothing about whether its captured object still exists. Parameters can be named explicitly or inferred with $0; multiple nested shorthand closures can obscure which parameter belongs to which scope. Kotlin lambdas and trailing syntax provide an algorithm analogy, but Swift’s function types, external labels and ownership remain distinct rules.

sections.title: Allow a callback to outlive the installing call
sections.html:
An escaping closure may survive after the function receiving it returns. Install stores action in a property, so its plain closure parameter needs @escaping. The attribute belongs to that parameter, not the property’s function type. Button.action is an optional zero-input function returning Void, meaning no useful result. Tap calls it synchronously if present. Clearing action removes Button’s ownership of the stored function. The first tap prints Tapped; after clearing, the second prints nothing. Longer lifetime permission says nothing about a background thread or guaranteed invocation.

final class Button {
    var action: (() -> Void)?

    func install(_ action: @escaping () -> Void) {
        self.action = action
    }

    func tap() {
        action?()
    }
}
let button = Button()
button.install { print("Tapped") }
button.tap()
button.action = nil
button.tap()

Ordinary closure parameters are nonescaping by default when used only during the call. An optional closure parameter has different type behavior and should not receive the same plain-parameter rule mechanically. Escaping permits a longer lifetime; it does not require storage, guarantee delivery, make the closure weak, or mean background execution. A named completion may still never be called unless the producer’s contract and implementation ensure it. Kotlin noinline/crossinline and callbacks address related concerns, but they are not exact equivalents to Swift’s escaping lifetime annotation. When bridging later APIs, analyze registration, execution context and cancellation separately instead of treating one keyword as all three.

sections.title: Break the strong circle when disappearance is allowed
sections.html:
A strong reference keeps a class instance alive. A weak reference observes it without ownership and becomes nil after release. Owner stores action; a closure strongly capturing that owner would complete a retention cycle, an owning circle. [weak self] removes that strong return edge. Guard then binds a present self strongly for this one invocation. Saved keeps the closure alive, but its weak capture does not keep Owner alive. The first call prints Synthetic. Removing the known strong owner makes probe nil, so true prints. The saved callback can still exist and safely return without an owner.

final class Owner {
    let name = "Synthetic"
    var action: (() -> Void)?

    func install() {
        action = { [weak self] in
            guard let self else { return }
            print(self.name)
        }
    }
}
func checkLifetime() {
    var owner: Owner? = Owner()
    owner?.install()
    let saved = owner?.action
    weak var probe = owner
    saved?()
    owner = nil
    print(probe == nil)
    saved?()
}
checkLifetime()

Deinit runs when a class instance is being released; it cannot fix a circle that prevents release from beginning. Break or weaken an owning edge first. Weak is useful when the owner may disappear and the body can handle that. A deliberate strong capture may be right when another owner must keep finite work alive. Ordinary unowned is also non-owning, but accessing it after its target is released traps; use it only with a proven lifetime relationship. Keep a crashing demonstration out of the passing program. Weak capture is not cancellation. Work can continue without its receiver, and a living screen can already be inactive.

sections.title: Choose a live binding or a captured value
sections.html:
A snapshot records a value at one moment. The live closure captures the mutable local label binding and reads its later value when called. The capture list [label] records the String at closure creation instead. Updating label to After therefore gives After from live and Before from snapshot. A named capture such as [initial = label] can make intent clearer. Capturing a class reference records that reference, not a deep copy or frozen object. The String test input isolates the capture choice so the results are easy to predict.

func compareCaptures() {
    var label = "Before"
    let live = { print(label) }
    let snapshot = { [label] in print(label) }
    label = "After"
    live()
    snapshot()
}
compareCaptures()

After guard unwraps weak self, the local self is strong while used by the body. If an inner stored closure captures that local binding, it may retain the owner strongly. Its capture policy is separate; outer weak capture does not spread automatically to nested closures or tasks. Draw storage and release for each layer. Bounded temporary ownership is different from a circle with no release path. Optimization and last use can affect the precise source line where destruction happens. A weak probe, after deliberately removing known strong owners, is better evidence than assuming deinit always prints at one fixed line.

sections.title: Draw each stored closure’s own ownership
sections.html:
An ownership graph shows who strongly keeps whom alive. The linked coordinator stores an async throwing callback and accepts it as escaping. Its installed callback captures self weakly, binds it strongly with guard, and starts a Task using that strong binding. Task is a unit of asynchronous work; those scheduling rules need later study. An inner closure has its own capture choices, so the outer weak capture does not make every nested use weak. These source lines show ownership shape. They do not prove prompt task completion or cancellation when a screen disappears.

Misconceptions include reading escaping as background, weak as cancellation, a capture list as recursive cloning, and an outer weak capture as a nested policy. Draw the actual owning arrows and ask where each stored function value is released. An intentional strong-cycle experiment should explicitly clear the closure afterward through a weak probe, so it does not leave its own leak behind. The optional callback-ownership supplement expands notification tokens, delegates and queues after these prerequisites. It is matching further reading rather than a required advanced lesson. Today’s deterministic lifetime test has no sleeps, real events or networking and leaves learner completion unchanged.

steps: Create an owner with an optional () -> Void action and an install method.

exercise.solution:
This standalone check increments a count while Recorder exists. A weak probe observes whether it survives after the known strong owner is removed. Predict the output before running. Check closure presence and captured-owner presence as two separate questions.

final class Recorder {
    var count = 0
    var action: (() -> Void)?
    func install() {
        action = { [weak self] in
            guard let self else { return }
            self.count += 1
            print(self.count)
        }
    }
}
func check() {
    var recorder: Recorder? = Recorder()
    recorder?.install()
    let saved = recorder?.action
    weak var probe = recorder
    saved?()
    recorder = nil
    print(probe == nil)
    saved?()
}
check()

Output is one then true. The second invocation of saved finds a nil weak owner and returns. The optional invocation only checks that saved itself exists; the guard handles the separate owner question. The initializer accepts no closure parameter, so @escaping is unnecessary here even though the property stores a constructed closure.

For an intentional cycle variant, replace the weak capture with a strong self capture, predict probe staying nonnil after recorder is cleared, and then clear probe?.action to release the cycle. That is a separate negative ownership experiment with cleanup, not a compiler failure. Repeat the live/snapshot String exercise with changed values to demonstrate capture transfer. These language checks do not establish notification removal, async producer cancellation, actor safety, or learner mastery.

lessons.title: Use protocols and keep useful type relationships
lessons.summary: Describe shared capabilities with protocols, preserve type relationships with generics, and read any, some, and Self.
objectives: Declare a protocol requirement and a generic function with the constraint it needs.
Tell unrestricted Any, protocol-bound any, and generic or opaque some apart.
Explain associated types, Self, and why a protocol helper can behave differently from a requirement.

sections.title: Name the capability a caller needs
sections.html:
A protocol lists capabilities a type must provide. A requirement is a member promised by that list. Conformance means a type meets the requirements; a colon after its name can declare that promise. A struct, class, or enum can conform. var title: String { get } promises readable text, not stored mutable state. This resembles an Android interface. Generics address a different question: which types must relate? A generic type parameter names a type within a declaration so inputs and results can preserve that relationship without being reduced to unrestricted Any.

A generic type parameter is a locally named type relationship, not the unrestricted Any container. A function identity<T>(_ value: T) -> T preserves the input type in its output. The caller chooses a suitable T through arguments/context. Operations on T require declared constraints; equality needs Equatable, and ordering needs a suitable comparison contract. Kotlin’s generic syntax is useful for intent, but Swift constraints, associated types and existential rules differ from JVM erasure/reified assumptions. Start with the API information the caller needs. Do not choose a type-erasure mechanism merely because an error message mentions generics.

sections.title: Keep one named type throughout a generic call
sections.html:
A generic parameter such as T stands for a type chosen for a call. Angle brackets declare it. Identity takes T and returns the same T, so an Int input gives an Int result and a String input gives a String result without a cast. A constraint limits which types qualify. T: Equatable requires value equality so same can use ==. Both of its inputs share T; an existing Int and an existing String do not fit that promise together. The outputs are 3, Ada, true, and false.

func identity<T>(_ value: T) -> T {
    return value
}
func same<T: Equatable>(_ left: T, _ right: T) -> Bool {
    return left == right
}
let number: Int = identity(3)
let text: String = identity("Ada")
print(number)
print(text)
print(same(3, 3))
print(same("Ada", "Rae"))

A where clause adds type constraints, such as requiring two associated element types to match. == between types in that clause means same type, not runtime value equality. Ask only for the capabilities the algorithm uses; unnecessary constraints exclude useful callers. Specialization means the compiler may generate code for a concrete type, but it is an optimization possibility rather than a promised speedup. Equatable supplies value comparison, not hashing, object identity, copying, or thread safety. Kotlin has no exact named Equatable contract with identical rules. Keep value equality and a product’s lasting record identity as separate decisions.

sections.title: Declare the member that must vary by conformer
sections.html:
Dispatch is the rule for choosing which method implementation runs. Greeting declares message as a requirement. Its extension, added behavior for an existing type or protocol, supplies a default message and a helper decoration. CustomGreeting supplies its own versions. Direct concrete decoration returns Concrete. Through a generic Greeting constraint or an existential any Greeting value, message selects the conformer’s required implementation, but decoration selects the extension helper. Decoration was never a requirement. The combined results are Custom/Extension in both calls. Matching method names alone do not create the missing promise.

protocol Greeting {
    func message() -> String
}
extension Greeting {
    func message() -> String { "Default" }
    func decoration() -> String { "Extension" }
}
struct CustomGreeting: Greeting {
    func message() -> String { "Custom" }
    func decoration() -> String { "Concrete" }
}
func throughGeneric<G: Greeting>(_ value: G) -> String {
    return value.message() + "/" + value.decoration()
}
let concrete = CustomGreeting()
let erased: any Greeting = concrete
print(concrete.decoration())
print(throughGeneric(concrete))
print(erased.message() + "/" + erased.decoration())

If decoration must vary through Greeting, add it to the protocol requirements and optionally retain the extension default. An extension can add methods, computed properties, and conformances, but not stored instance properties. Kotlin extension functions help explain static helper selection. Swift additionally uses requirement witnesses, the implementations chosen to fulfill a conformance. Inherited class conformances and method overrides add subtleties, so this simple struct test input is not a rule for every subclass. Test the generic or existential boundary that the actual consumer uses, not just concrete calls. A protocol does not imply its conformers are classes.

sections.title: Read any and some from the caller’s contract
sections.html:
An existential value, written any Naming, holds a concrete conformer behind the protocol’s declared capabilities. Different entries can hold different conforming types, as Person and Place do here. Uppercase Any allows unrelated types and promises little without inspection. An opaque result, written some Naming, hides one concrete result type chosen by the function while preserving its type identity. Its ordinary return paths must use that same underlying type. Parameter-position some means a generic constrained input instead. The word’s position changes who chooses the concrete type.

protocol Naming {
    var name: String { get }
}
struct Person: Naming { let name: String }
struct Place: Naming { let name: String }
func chosenPerson() -> some Naming {
    return Person(name: "Ada")
}
func caption(_ value: some Naming) -> String {
    return value.name
}
let mixed: [any Naming] = [Person(name: "Ada"), Place(name: "Park")]
print(chosenPerson().name)
for value in mixed { print(value.name) }
print(caption(Person(name: "Rae")))

An input written some Naming is shorthand for a generic parameter constrained to Naming. Two separate some inputs do not require one shared concrete type; name a common T if that relationship is required. Kotlin interface values help explain substituting conformers, but Swift’s hidden result type and associated-type relationships need their own rules. Opaque parameter syntax is supported from Swift 5.7; the course scratch baseline is Swift 6 or newer. The outputs are Ada, Ada, Park, and Rae. Existential storage may involve boxing or indirect dispatch depending on representation. Choose the required API contract first, then measure relevant code rather than promising a fixed cost.

sections.title: Preserve the related element type and the returned type
sections.html:
An associated type names a type selected by each protocol conformance. Source names Element; its primary associated type list allows convenient constraints such as any Source<Int>. ArraySource stores [Value], so Swift infers its Element to be Value. First returns S.Element?, keeping the source’s element type while allowing an empty source. The constrained existential hides the source implementation but retains Int as its element type. Uppercase Self means the current or conforming type; lowercase self means an instance. Note returns a new Note through Self, preserving that result relationship.

protocol Source<Element> {
    associatedtype Element
    var items: [Element] { get }
}
struct ArraySource<Value>: Source {
    let items: [Value]
}
func first<S: Source>(_ source: S) -> S.Element? {
    return source.items.first
}
protocol ReplacingTitle {
    func replacingTitle(_ text: String) -> Self
}
struct Note: ReplacingTitle {
    let title: String
    func replacingTitle(_ text: String) -> Self {
        return Self(title: text)
    }
}
let source = ArraySource(items: [2, 4])
let known: any Source<Int> = source
print(first(source) ?? -1)
print(known.items.count)
print(Note(title: "Before").replacingTitle("After").title)

Note’s Self result preserves its own type when it constructs a new value. Lowercase self would refer to a particular instance instead. Neither spelling promises to clone nested class objects. Class factories also have inheritance and initialization obligations not shown by this struct. The outputs are 2, 2, and After. Some existential operations are limited when associated relationships remain unknown; modern Swift can open some existential values for generic calls. The generic-contracts guide expands these rules, where clauses, and class dispatch after this lesson. State which relationship you need to keep instead of assuming any always loses every fact or can recover all hidden relationships.

sections.title: Read constraints as permission to do work
sections.html:
A constraint is a promise the algorithm can rely on. The sequence helper asks its sort key to be Comparable, meaning it supports ordering, and its uniqueness key to be Hashable, meaning it supports equality and hashing. The whole input element need not have those capabilities. The selectedOption extension also requires Element to be one specific model type; that is a same-type condition. GooglePlaceDetailsServing declares a protocol requirement with async, throws, and Sendable effects. Those add suspension, failure, and concurrency-transfer rules for later study. Read the labels and capability here without claiming the surrounding system is verified.

Misconceptions include treating T as Any, thinking every any wraps a class, expecting some to return unrelated concrete types, and assuming an extension-only helper dynamically specializes. Classify missing constraints and mismatched types as compiler failures, while the wrong helper selection is valid code with a misleading API contract. Test concrete, generic and existential access before declaring substitution correct. We verified anchors and module membership, not generic specialization performance or a repository-wide any migration. The exercise uses standalone pure types so the caller-visible relationships, not framework complexity, decide the design.

exercise.solution:
This complete file demonstrates requirement dispatch and helper selection. For the source’s element type, use the separate complete associated-source example above. Predict all four lines before running. In particular, compare the direct helper call with the helper called through a protocol constraint.

protocol Captioning { func caption() -> String }
extension Captioning {
    func caption() -> String { "Default" }
    func helper() -> String { "Extension" }
}
struct Badge: Captioning {
    func caption() -> String { "Custom" }
    func helper() -> String { "Concrete" }
}
func inspect<C: Captioning>(_ value: C) -> String {
    value.caption() + "/" + value.helper()
}
let badge = Badge()
let erased: any Captioning = badge
print(badge.caption())
print(badge.helper())
print(inspect(badge))
print(erased.caption() + "/" + erased.helper())

Output is Custom, Concrete, Custom/Extension and Custom/Extension. If helper must specialize, add it as a requirement and rerun boundary calls. That change alters the API contract, not merely spelling. Explain why a concrete-only assertion would have missed the consumer’s behavior.

For the source task, first(ArraySource(items: [Int]())) returns nil while a nonempty integer source returns Int?. Any provides unrestricted storage, any provides a protocol-bound value, result some hides one chosen implementation type, and Self links behavior to the conforming type. These explanations are intentionally bounded; associated-type variance, inherited witnesses and ABI optimization require further specialist practice. Record independent predictions and runs rather than counting this answer as completion.

lessons.summary: Combine value copies, collections, error reasons, and weak callbacks. Test what the core promises and record what still needs practice.
