Separate compiler checks, executed expectations, and platform integration evidence.

sections.title: Write expected behavior before choosing code
sections.html:
A behavior contract states what a program should do for named inputs. Write one for this quantity-import exercise before opening earlier answers. Editing a draft must preserve the original. Accepted text must spell a positive integer. Empty input is still a successful result. Malformed text and nonpositive numbers need different failure reasons. A saved refresh callback must handle its owner being gone. These are observable requirements you can test using your Android unit-test experience. Use made-up inputs, then choose language features that express the rules. Completing this lesson alone is not a certification.

The core remains synchronous and independent of UI, networking, actors and persistence. Cancellation and freshness have distinct host workshops later, so do not infer those guarantees from a weak callback. Write a prediction sheet with certain, tentative and guessed answers for assignment, argument labels, optional conversion, enum payloads and capture lifetime. Then implement before opening the worked core. Passing authored examples supports their language behavior; your own changed-input implementation demonstrates transfer. Any unfinished attempt remains pending. A useful handoff identifies what you can now explain and the two rules you still need to retrieve under new test inputs.

sections.title: Read the complete core one responsibility at a time
sections.html:
A replaceable boundary lets a caller supply another implementation of a promised capability. Parsing is that protocol here. Draft stores input as an array value. LabFailure carries named error reasons, and Outcome distinguishes idle, loaded, and failed. Parser visits each text in order and throws at the first invalid row: the whole batch succeeds or fails. CompactMap would instead drop failures and change the rule. Place the full code in Sources/BootcampCore/Core.swift for the package, or combine it with the smoke check as one file. It needs only the Swift standard library.

struct Draft: Equatable {
    var texts: [String]
}
enum LabFailure: Error, Equatable {
    case invalid(String)
    case nonpositive(Int)
    case unexpected
}
enum Outcome: Equatable {
    case idle
    case loaded([Int])
    case failed(LabFailure)
}
protocol Parsing {
    func parse(_ texts: [String]) throws -> [Int]
}
struct Parser: Parsing {
    func parse(_ texts: [String]) throws -> [Int] {
        var values: [Int] = []
        for text in texts {
            guard let value = Int(text) else { throw LabFailure.invalid(text) }
            guard value > 0 else { throw LabFailure.nonpositive(value) }
            values.append(value)
        }
        return values
    }
}
func load(_ draft: Draft, using parser: any Parsing) -> Outcome {
    do {
        return .loaded(try parser.parse(draft.texts))
    } catch let failure as LabFailure {
        return .failed(failure)
    } catch {
        return .failed(.unexpected)
    }
}
final class Owner {
    var draft: Draft
    let parser: any Parsing
    private(set) var outcome: Outcome = .idle
    var refresh: (() -> Void)?

    init(draft: Draft, parser: any Parsing) {
        self.draft = draft
        self.parser = parser
        self.refresh = { [weak self] in
            guard let self else { return }
            self.outcome = load(self.draft, using: self.parser)
        }
    }
}

Load receives any Parsing, so it uses the protocol’s parse capability without requiring one concrete parser type. Its catch for LabFailure keeps the known reason; unrelated errors become unexpected, not empty success. Owner is a class so this exercise can study shared lifetime. It owns draft, parser, and refresh, while refresh captures the owner weakly. The guard holds a present owner strongly for that synchronous call. Private(set) limits outcome writes while allowing normal internal reads. These declarations default to internal visibility. Throws permits failure; it does not select a background executor. The core needs no company dependency resolver or companion-package function.

sections.title: Put the core and tests in separate targets
sections.html:
A package manifest describes what to build. A target is one buildable component, and a module is the unit another component imports. Put this manifest at your scratch package root, core code under Sources/BootcampCore, and tests under Tests/BootcampCoreTests. The header requires Swift tools 6.0 or later; swiftLanguageModes selects Swift 6 checks. Dependencies is empty. The library product exposes the core target, and the test target depends on it. PackageDescription belongs to the manifest. Testing belongs to the tests and supplies macros, compiler-supported syntax used below for tests and expectations.

// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "BootcampCore",
    products: [.library(name: "BootcampCore", targets: ["BootcampCore"])],
    dependencies: [],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "BootcampCore"),
        .testTarget(name: "BootcampCoreTests", dependencies: ["BootcampCore"])
    ],
    swiftLanguageModes: [.v6]
)

The core uses internal APIs. @testable import allows the tests to use those APIs in a testing-enabled build; it does not generally bypass private access. An ordinary importing module would need explicit public declarations and construction APIs. A library product does not automatically make members public. Keep Testing macros in the test target: a standalone source run does not discover them. From the scratch package root, swift test builds the modules and runs discovered tests. Use isolated temporary caches if needed in a restricted host. Report the environment actually used; a newer macOS toolchain run proves neither the minimum toolchain nor Linux, simulator, or company-app behavior.

sections.title: Give each test an observable promise
sections.html:
A test runs a small scenario and checks an expected result. @Test declares a Swift Testing function; #expect records whether an observation matches the rule. The first test checks copy independence. The second checks both populated and empty success. The third checks the two rejection reasons. The fourth replaces the parser with a fake that throws another error and expects unexpected failure. The fifth saves a callback, calls it while its owner exists, removes that owner, checks a weak probe, and calls again safely. Each test creates its own local inputs and needs no shared execution order.

import Testing
@testable import BootcampCore

@Test func editsPreserveOriginal() {
    let original = Draft(texts: ["2"])
    var edited = original
    edited.texts.append("3")
    #expect(original.texts == ["2"])
    #expect(edited.texts == ["2", "3"])
}
@Test func successAndEmptyStaySuccessful() {
    #expect(load(Draft(texts: ["2", "3"]), using: Parser()) == .loaded([2, 3]))
    #expect(load(Draft(texts: []), using: Parser()) == .loaded([]))
}
@Test func failuresKeepTheirReasons() {
    #expect(load(Draft(texts: ["bad"]), using: Parser()) == .failed(.invalid("bad")))
    #expect(load(Draft(texts: ["0"]), using: Parser()) == .failed(.nonpositive(0)))
}
enum OtherFailure: Error { case offline }
struct FailingParser: Parsing {
    func parse(_ texts: [String]) throws -> [Int] { throw OtherFailure.offline }
}
@Test func unexpectedFailureIsNotSuccess() {
    #expect(load(Draft(texts: []), using: FailingParser()) == .failed(.unexpected))
}
@Test func savedCallbackToleratesRelease() {
    var owner: Owner? = Owner(draft: Draft(texts: ["2"]), parser: Parser())
    let saved = owner?.refresh
    weak var probe = owner
    saved?()
    #expect(owner?.outcome == .loaded([2]))
    owner = nil
    #expect(probe == nil)
    saved?()
}

A macro supplies compiler-supported syntax; @Test and #expect come from Testing, rather than being preprocessor directives or language-only assert spellings. The testable import allows internal access in this build and still requires the test target’s dependency on the core. The owner-release test uses no sleep because its behavior is synchronous. Waiting would add delay without creating an event it needs. XCTest is another common test framework with different declaration and assertion APIs. This scratch suite follows the Swift Testing pattern found in the linked active repository tests. Keep compilation and executed test success as separate observations in the record.

sections.title: Name exactly which check you ran
sections.html:
A smoke check is a small executable check of key behavior. Combine the complete core block with this block in one standalone file. Run with assertions enabled: some optimization modes disable assert. The message Language checks passed appears only after these synchronous assertions succeed. This route does not discover Swift Testing functions; the package suite does and additionally checks unexpected failure. A file containing only declarations may compile without exercising anything. Record whether you ran the standalone check or the package tests, plus the toolchain, command, and observed result.

func check() {
    let original = Draft(texts: ["2"])
    var edited = original
    edited.texts.append("3")
    assert(original.texts == ["2"])
    assert(load(edited, using: Parser()) == .loaded([2, 3]))
    assert(load(Draft(texts: []), using: Parser()) == .loaded([]))
    assert(load(Draft(texts: ["bad"]), using: Parser()) == .failed(.invalid("bad")))
    assert(load(Draft(texts: ["0"]), using: Parser()) == .failed(.nonpositive(0)))
    var owner: Owner? = Owner(draft: edited, parser: Parser())
    let saved = owner?.refresh
    weak var probe = owner
    saved?()
    assert(owner?.outcome == .loaded([2, 3]))
    owner = nil
    assert(probe == nil)
    saved?()
    print("Language checks passed")
}
check()

Use a separate private scratch version to try a known wrong rule: make every catch return loaded empty output. Predict the failed expectations before running, then restore the classification. Also predict a strong capture circle. The weak probe would stay nonnil until the stored closure is cleared; give that experiment an explicit cleanup. These are different failures: rejected code, failed expectations, and retained ownership. A same-variable inout conflict from lesson 064 belongs in a separate compiler-rejection example, not the passing suite. Label each deliberate negative so a reviewer can tell it from an accidental bug.

sections.title: Repeat with new inputs and keep the limits visible
sections.html:
A companion package is separate practice code. SwiftLanguageLab has its own library, swift-workbench executable, and test target in Swift 6 mode. It has no remote dependencies. Read its manifest and README before calling its functions. Those files describe commands with isolated caches, its language examples, event gates, and Foundation practice. BootcampCore above has a separate complete API; do not assume the two packages expose interchangeable functions. The companion’s public construction APIs differ from this testable internal module. Its Foundation test input exercises belong to their own workshop.

Retrieval practice means recalling a rule before opening its answer. Trace the linked question model, enum wrapper, stored callback, and test source pattern; say what each line establishes. Then predict new inputs in your own core, such as a negative number or several positive rows. Repeat in two days and a week with changed inputs and the answer closed. Record limits: host tests do not check screen lifecycle, platform availability, module distribution, actor isolation, cancellation, serialization, or real error reporting. Leave earlier quiz and progress records as they are. Choose further practice from mistaken predictions rather than declaring the whole language mastered.

The exercised core behaviors passed on the recorded host/toolchain
quiz.explanation: Verification is scoped to the code, fixtures and environment actually executed. Independent transfer and platform checks remain separate.

quiz.question: Why does empty input yield loaded([])?
options: Empty input is a successful result under this contract
All errors should become empty arrays
Enums require arrays to be nonempty
quiz.explanation: Success with zero rows is distinct from invalid/domain/unexpected failure and from idle. The tests protect that domain distinction.

quiz.question: Why does the test target use @testable import?
options: The core APIs are internal and testing-enabled access is intentional
It exports private members to every app
quiz.explanation: The test build can access internal declarations. It still needs a target dependency and does not generally expose private APIs.

exercise.brief: Build your own quantity core and tests, record predictions and actual results, and choose two rules to practise again.
steps: Write a behavior table before reading the answer.
Create your own scratch core and test target, or one combined standalone file.
Use value input, distinct outcomes, a replaceable throwing parser, and a stored weak-owner refresh callback.
Check copied edits, populated and empty success, malformed and nonpositive input, unexpected failure, and owner release.
In a separate scratch version, turn errors into empty success. Predict which test fails, run it, then restore the correct rule.
Read the companion README before running its package. Record that run separately.
Later, repeat the two concepts you understand least with new inputs. Leave unattempted learner work pending.
acceptance: All declared output distinctions have independently authored assertions or explicit paper predictions.
A saved callback can outlive a released owner without a cycle or crash.
The record distinguishes compile, test execution and any companion run.
No existing quiz/checklist indices or learner completion are altered.
The handoff lists two remaining practice goals and verification limits rather than automatic mastery.
exercise.solution:
The full core, manifest, and test block above form the package answer. The core plus smoke block form the standalone answer. Choose the route matching your scratch layout and record the toolchain, command, exit result, and final summary. The package defines five Swift Testing tests. Its runner may also report zero XCTest tests in a compatibility preamble; read the final Swift Testing summary before deciding whether the five functions ran.

The deliberate errors-to-empty mutation should fail malformed, nonpositive and unexpected-failure expectations while successful empty input still passes. That shows the tests defend domain distinctions instead of mirroring implementation structure. Restore explicit classification before keeping your completed scratch answer. The lifetime test establishes a weak owning edge and safe missing-owner path; it proves no producer cancellation because the program has no producer work.

For a changed exercise, parse [4, 6] and predict loaded([4, 6]), then parse [-1] and predict failed(nonpositive(-1)). Explain how an accept-valid-rows policy would require an output carrying rejection evidence rather than merely changing compactMap. Optional matching guides can deepen construction, generic contracts and callback ownership afterward. Author verification does not pre-complete the learner’s attempt; readiness depends on independent implementation, explained predictions and a documented remaining-practice plan.

simple.story: Ada receives two shopping slips marked 2 and 3. Her rule is to accept the whole bundle only when every slip shows a positive whole number. An empty bundle is a successful request for nothing. A slip marked bad gets a different report from a slip marked zero. Before using the rule, Ada checks examples for all four situations. She also keeps the original bundle when making an edited copy, so reviewing an edit does not change the earlier record.
simple.meaning: The integrated core protects distinct outcomes with tests. It rejects the whole batch on invalid input, while successful empty input remains loaded([]).

example.before: Draft contains ["2", "3"]. Parser accepts positive integer text. A separate empty Draft contains [].
example.change: Call load on each Draft using Parser, then try a Draft containing ["bad"].
example.after: The results are loaded([2, 3]), loaded([]), and failed(invalid("bad")). Empty success and rejected text remain different states.

picture.caption: Independent test cases protect distinct results rather than one shared execution sequence.
